metadata.title: US House passes short-term funding bill to avert government shutdown before midterm elections

sources.news_title: The 370-48 vote keeps federal agencies funded at current levels and gives lawmakers more time to negotiate full-year spending bills.
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The House voted Tuesday to keep the federal government funded through Dec. 11, sending a short-term spending bill to President Donald Trump and pushing the threat of a shutdown past the November midterm elections.
The measure passed 370-48. The Senate approved the same legislation 90-6 last month. Trump is expected to sign it.
The continuing resolution would keep most federal agencies operating at current spending levels after the new fiscal year begins Oct. 1. Current funding expires Sept. 30. Lawmakers have not completed the 12 annual appropriations bills that normally fund the government for a full year.
House leaders brought the Senate-passed bill to the floor under suspension of the rules, an expedited process that requires a two-thirds majority and limits amendments. The lopsided tally reflected broad bipartisan support for avoiding a funding fight during the campaign season. Nineteen Republicans and 29 Democrats voted no, according to vote tallies reported after the roll call.
The legislation is H.R. 6500, the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027. It funds the government through Dec. 11 or until full-year appropriations are enacted, whichever comes first.
Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters before the vote that Republicans intended to “avoid the threat of another Democratic shutdown.” Majority Leader Steve Scalise said lawmakers still want a longer-term deal but needed to keep the government functioning in the meantime.
House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole said the vote followed work House Republicans began earlier in the summer.
“Today’s vote is the culmination of House Republicans moving proactively, decisively, and strategically earlier this summer. The action we took paved the way for the Senate to promptly engage in the process, and I am proud to say we are now sending this funding extension to President Trump without waiting for the clock to run out,” Cole said in a statement. “Responsible governance means putting the well-being and stability of the nation first, and this legislation does just that. It protects our national security, preserves critical services, and denies partisan shutdown agitators the leverage they have repeatedly sought.”
“The bill is simple by design – no poison pills, no divisive wish lists, and no political gimmicks,” Cole added. “Just a clean, straightforward measure that keeps the government working, provides more time to address full-year bills, and trades the familiar cycle of Senate Democrat brinkmanship for something far more useful: certainty.”
Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger framed the outcome as a governing choice.
“House Republicans came to Washington to govern, and today we did just that by keeping the government open and avoiding another Democrat-manufactured shutdown despite the Left trying to hold the process hostage,” Pfluger said. “We have a responsibility to keep the government funded and operating, and we take that seriously as we continue the work of finishing full year conservative appropriations.”
The Senate version differs from a House-passed stopgap adopted in July that would have run only through Dec. 4 and drew far less Democratic support.
The bill also delays for about a month a federal ban on intoxicating hemp products scheduled to take effect in November, a change sought by the White House. That provision drew opposition from some House conservatives, including members of the Freedom Caucus, who also objected to the grants language and to considering the bill under suspension.
The stopgap does not resolve the larger fight over fiscal 2027 spending. House committees have advanced appropriations bills, but the Senate has not passed its counterparts. Cole and other Republicans said the extra time would allow Congress to finish full-year bills after the Nov. 3 elections, when control of both chambers will be at stake.
Congress has relied on continuing resolutions for years as the two parties have struggled to complete regular appropriations on time. Lawmakers cited last year’s lengthy shutdowns as a reason they did not want another funding lapse to collide with the midterm campaign.
If Trump signs the bill, federal agencies, Social Security payments, military pay, nutrition assistance and other core operations would continue under existing terms into mid-December. The next deadline would then fall just before the holiday season, when the newly elected Congress and the White House would face another round of negotiations over full-year funding.

US House passes stopgap funding bill to avert shutdown until 11 December
The House passed a stopgap funding bill to keep the US government open until 11 December. The move averts an immediate shutdown but defers a bitter spending fight until after the campaign stretch.
The US House of Representatives on Tuesday passed a short-term funding bill to keep the federal government running until December 11, in a move aimed at avoiding a shutdown as lawmakers campaign for re-election. The bill was passed 370-48 and now goes to President Donald Trump for his signature after already being approved by the Senate.
Lawmakers had to act before the fiscal year ends in late September to prevent a funding lapse. Both parties were keen to avoid another disruption during the campaign season after a series of long shutdowns and funding standoffs over the past year, even as wider differences over government spending remain unresolved.
Republican Rep. Tom Cole, chairman of the House Appropriations Committee, said the measure would provide stability. “It gives the nation and our constituents certainty, certainty that the government will remain open, certainty that our service members will be paid,” he said.
Lawmakers were wary of a repeat of last year’s record 43-day shutdown, which happened after Republicans and Democrats disagreed over renewing a tax credit that reduces the cost of health coverage bought through Affordable Care Act marketplaces. That was followed by a 76-day shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security before lawmakers agreed to fund much of the department, but not its immigration enforcement operations. Both parties blamed each other for those deadlocks. Before the vote, House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters, “We’re going to avoid the threat of another Democratic shutdown.” After the vote, he said the House had delivered despite doubts over whether the Republican majority could overcome its own divisions. “We’re continuing to do the grown-up thing, get the job done,” he said.
Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, urged her party colleagues in a closed-door meeting on Tuesday morning to support the bill. She said it was much better than the version the House passed earlier this summer on a mostly party-line basis. She said the revised bill stops the Department of Homeland Security from moving funds to the Border Patrol and delays a proposed rule that would give Trump administration political appointees more power to block federal grants for programmes they believe do not match the president’s agenda. Those changes were made after the Senate passed its version of the bill.
Democrats said they were concerned the proposed grants rule could be used to divert money away from states led by Democrats. DeLauro said delaying it was an important first step, but added that more must be done to stop the policy from taking effect. “Whether a community receives disaster relief should not depend on who they voted for in the last election,” she said. The temporary bill keeps federal agencies funded at current levels through December 11 and gives lawmakers more time to negotiate a full-year spending plan, though that is expected to be difficult as Republicans push for hundreds of billions of dollars more for the military and cuts to most non-defence programmes, while Democrats insist on a bipartisan approach with equal treatment for domestic spending.
In effect, the House vote has pushed back the immediate threat of a government shutdown, while leaving the larger battle over full-year federal spending for later in the year.
With PTI Inputs

The House passed a short-term measure Tuesday to fund the federal government into early December, a move designed to avoid a chaotic shutdown as lawmakers campaign for reelection.
Lawmakers needed to act before the fiscal year concludes at the end of September to avoid a funding lapse. They were determined not to bump up against that deadline during the campaign season following this past year’s historic shutdowns.
The House passed the bill by a vote of 370-48. The Senate has already overwhelmingly approved the measure, so it now moves to President Donald Trump’s desk for his signature.
“It gives the nation and our constituents certainty, certainty that the government will remain open, certainty that our service members will be paid,” said Rep. Tom Cole, the Republican chairman of the House Appropriations Committee.
A record 43-day shutdown occurred last fall when the two parties disagreed on renewing an expiring tax credit that lowers the cost of health coverage obtained through Affordable Care Act marketplaces. Then came the shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security, which lasted 76 days before lawmakers agreed to fund much of the department but not its immigration enforcement operations.
Lawmakers were wary of a repeat before voters go to the polls. They also blamed the other party for the recent impasses.
“We’re going to avoid the threat of another Democratic shutdown,” House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters in advance of the vote.
After the vote Johnson said the House delivered, despite those who doubted the Republican majority would be able to push past its own divisions and rally support.
“We’re continuing to do the grown-up thing, get the job done,” he said.
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the lead Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, encouraged her Democratic colleagues to vote for the measure during a closed-door meeting Tuesday morning.
She said the bill was much improved from the product that passed the House earlier this summer on a mostly party-line basis. For example, she said it prevents the Department of Homeland Security from transferring funds to the Border Patrol, and it delays a proposed rule that would give political appointees in the Trump administration more authority to stop federal grants from going out for programs they view as not in line with the president’s agenda. Those changes were made when the Senate approved its version of the bill.
Democrats fear the administration will use the proposed regulation on grants to steer money away from Democratic-led states. DeLauro called the delay an important first step, but said more must be done to block the policy from taking effect.
“Whether a community receives disaster relief should not depend on who they voted for in the last election,” DeLauro said.
The short-term measure funds federal agencies generally at current levels through Dec. 11. It will give lawmakers more time to find compromise on a full-year measure, though that will likely be quite difficult.
Republicans are seeking hundreds of billions of dollars in additional spending for the military while cutting most non-defense programs. Democrats say that’s a non-starter and insist on a bipartisan approach that treats domestic programs with parity.

Associated Press writer Lisa Mascaro contributed.

US House clears spending stopgap backed by Trump, averting government shutdown
The U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — The U.S. House approved a short-term government funding bill Tuesday that would avoid a shutdown this fall once President Donald Trump signs it.
The 370-48 vote showed neither Republicans nor Democrats want a repeat of the funding lapse that took place last year when disagreement over enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits led to a historic 43-day shutdown.
The stopgap spending bill, which the Senate approved in early August, would provide mostly flat funding for federal departments and agencies to keep up and running from the start of the new fiscal year on Oct. 1 through Dec. 11.
The short-term funding patch is supposed to give Congress more time to reach bipartisan agreement on the dozen annual appropriations bills. Absent that, lawmakers can pass a series of stopgap spending bills or force another government shutdown.
House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said during floor debate the bill doesn’t include any “poison pills” or “partisan riders.”
“The bill before us is a clean, narrowly tailored continuing resolution that keeps the government open and operating. Nothing more. Nothing less,” he said. “It gives the nation and our constituents certainty.”
The measure, Cole said, would “allow Congress time to get past the November elections and allow us time to assess and move forward with further appropriations measures in November and December.”
Connecticut Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro, ranking member on the committee, said the bill doesn’t include any additional funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and would block the administration from moving any of the money to the Border Patrol.
Republicans in Congress approved a $70 billion package earlier this year intended to fund ICE and the Border Patrol for the next three years. That funding was on top of the roughly $170 billion for immigration enforcement included in the GOP’s “big, beautiful” law.
“We will not support a single cent in further funding without substantial reforms to protect our communities from abuse,” DeLauro said during debate.
The stopgap spending bill, she said, “is in no way a substitute for the full-year funding process. It is merely a means to complete this important work while averting a lapse in government funding.”
Senate action
Senators voted 96-0 to approve the spending measure in early August after making changes to a bill the House passed in late July.
The White House indicated last month that Trump plans to sign the bill when it reaches his desk, writing in a Statement of Administration Policy that the president “strongly opposes another futile Government shutdown.”
“Every Member of Congress should support passage of this CR to keep the Government open as discussions on full-year appropriations continue,” it said.
The current version of the legislation “closes the loophole that would have allowed the Trump administration to transfer funding for other programs to Border Patrol” and “extends authorizations of important health, veterans, infrastructure, and other programs,” according to a summary from Senate Appropriations Committee ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash.
Rule on grantmaking blocked
The bill also blocks the White House budget office from moving forward during the next few months with a rule that would give political appointees more influence over grants.
Senate Appropriations Chairwoman Susan Collins, R-Maine, wrote in a letter released in early July that “rule would impose new, burdensome requirements on award recipients that would harm small and rural communities, undermine scientific and biomedical research, and conflict with Congress’ control over the federal funding process.”
Democrats in Congress also oppose the proposed rule, arguing it “will make it impossible for grant recipients to faithfully carry out the funding priorities that Congress establishes in statute, and would turn federal grants into a new cudgel for the President to unilaterally advance his partisan agenda and punish political rivals.”
